item.title: Exercise for Your Mind
item.description:
Aging

Exercise for Your Mind

Research shows that book reading slows cognitive decline and enhances longevity.

Posted July 23, 2026

Key points
  • There is strong evidence that physical health contributes to longevity.
  • Research also shows a strong link between mental health and longevity.
  • Book reading has been shown to contribute to mental health and a long life.
"A Sound mind in a Sound Body"
Source: Szczecinolog, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

According to a study published last year (Santos-Pujol et al., 2025), the oldest living person in the world made it to 117 years, 168 days. That is a remarkably long life, and people are naturally very interested in just how she did it. Is it possible that the rest of us could make it to that admirable age? Just what would we need to do?

You’ve probably heard the old admonition that successful aging requires “a sound mind in a healthy body.” It is a quote from the Roman poet Juvenal (mens sana in corpore sano in Latin), usually used when someone is talking about the benefits of physical exercise to both health and well-being. If you ask your doctor how to age well, you’ll likely get advice about ways to keep your body healthy: eat right, get plenty of rest, avoid alcohol and smoking.

Santos-Pujol et al. conducted what is known as a multiomics study into the physical life of this remarkable woman. Multiomics refers to a cross-disciplinary examination of the DNA, RNA, proteins, metabolism, etc., of the physical health of a person. Many people assume that aging and physical health are negatively related to one another: As age increases, physical health declines. However, this particular woman proved to be physically healthy even at her very advanced age.

Keep in mind that the adage about sound bodies and minds also works the other way around. Successful aging also requires that we keep our minds strong and healthy to help us physically age in a healthy way. Recent research supports the idea that, along with maintaining a healthy diet and getting moderate exercise, a healthy social and leisure life is also essential to aging. Finding a way to keep your mind and your body engaged and active can help you live a long life.

Recent research has pointed to one particular leisure activity that is associated with longevity, one that many of us already enjoy: reading. At first blush, you wouldn’t necessarily think that reading, a fairly sedentary and quiet endeavor, would be associated with a longer lifespan, but the cognitive benefit that reading provides—the benefit to one’s mind—is the key factor. And interestingly, according to at least one study, it is not just reading but reading printed books in particular that is the most beneficial.

A (very) small portion of the bookshelves in my study.
Source: Barbara Blatchley

Bavishi, Slade, and Levy (2016) used a statistical technique that allows researchers to examine the association between the survival time of their participants and one or more predictor variables. The study followed more than 3,000 older participants for 12 years. The researchers tracked hours spent reading books per day, as well as magazine and newspaper reading time. They also looked at the contributions that “covariates” (factors that might also affect longevity, like age, sex, race, education level, general physical health, wealth, marital status, and depression) made to longevity. They found that book reading contributed to a survival advantage significantly more than did newspaper or magazine reading, and that “book readers also experienced a 20% reduction in risk of mortality over the 12 years of follow up compared to non-book readers.” Book reading was a “complete mediator” of the effect on longevity. When the mediator or predicting variable (book reading in this case) is dropped from the model, the statistic calculated in the model to measure the association between the predictor and risk of death drops to zero and no longer predicts longevity.

article continues after advertisement

Bavishi et al. speculate that reading books as opposed to magazines or newspapers creates a survival advantage for two reasons. First, books, more than magazines and newspapers, promote deep reading (Wolf, 2008) or a deep cognitive engagement with the material that allows the reader to make connections both within the book they’re immersed in and with things in the outside world. We use all of our senses, our memory, and our imagination when we are deeply reading. Citing a study that compared the writing in books vs. magazines and newspapers (Stanovich, 1992), Bavishi suggests that deep cognitive engagement is more likely with books than other kinds of reading material because of “the tendency of book authors to present themes, characters and topics in greater length and depth” and to use content to “promote empathy, social perception and emotional intelligence” (Bavishi et al.). Other researchers have noted that we receive kinesthetic and haptic (touch) feedback when we read books (Mangen, 2008), which is unavailable when we're reading on a Kindle or even in a magazine. Their size and weight tell us about length; we mark progress with our fingers or a bookmark; we flip back and forth to chase down ideas; we write notes in them, underline, highlight, and even claim them as ours with our names on the inside cover. This kind of interaction with the material is more difficult to do with a magazine or an e-book.

Finally, a large longitudinal study (almost 2,000 participants) in Taiwan tracked reading habits and cognitive function in older participants (64 years of age and up) across 14 years (Chang, Wu, and Hsiung, 2021). The researchers found that “[f]requent reading activities were associated with a reduced risk of cognitive decline for older adults at all levels of education in the long term.”

A long life with more time to read. Sounds good to me.

item.title: Why It Is So Hard to Say No to Your Struggling Adult Child
item.description:
Parenting

Why It Is So Hard to Say No to Your Struggling Adult Child

If you're not careful, today's help can become tomorrow's roadblock.

Posted July 23, 2026

Key points
  • Your brain sees the child, not the adult.
  • Guilt quietly hijacks good parenting.
  • You're afraid of losing the relationship.

Few things are more emotionally painful than watching your adult child struggle. If you are like many parents who reach out to me for coaching, you are saying to yourself, "They need the help." Let's be clear, I am not against parents helping out their adult children. But the adage, "Give a person a fish, they have dinner. Teach them how to fish, they never go hungry," comes to mind.

Whether your adult child is dealing with anxiety, depression, addiction, or emotional reactivity in general, or is simply having a hard time adulting, many parents get that nagging, "They need my help" sound bite reverberating loudly in their minds. By the way, while a lot of this post is about parents struggling to say no to financial requests and manipulation, it also addresses struggling to say no to being treated poorly and repeatedly accused of being the sole source of their children's difficulties.

Feeling like you should help (and unconditionally accept blame) may seem like you're being supportive, but it usually ends up being a trap. In my 35 years as a psychologist, I have worked with seemingly countless parents who have rescued their adult children. I'm talking about paying hundreds in parking tickets, thousands in rent, college tuition for adult children who have bailed on their classes, and many other painful stories. That's right, parents who get those crisis texts or calls slip into their first-responder (or, taking the metaphor to a higher intensity—SWAT team leader) uniforms and go on missions of mercy, motivated not by weakness but by love.

Why is saying no so difficult? Here are three reasons why.

1. You Still See the Child Behind the Adult

Your son may be 29, or your daughter may be 41, but part of you still probably sees the child who depended on you. That protective instinct does not disappear when children reach adulthood. So, when your adult child is hurting, your brain often responds as if it is your responsibility to make their pain go away. That's precisely why saying no can feel less like setting a boundary and more like abandoning someone you love. For example, when your 30-year-old daughter calls or texts saying she can't pay her rent (and you know she has a penchant for overdoing it with clothes shopping), it's easy to have your brain react as if she's still that frightened 10-year-old girl who needs you to make everything feel OK.

2. Guilt Can Override Good Judgment

Let's keep it real. Every parent has regrets. I have heard them all, such as maybe you worked too much, went through a rough divorce, or wish you had handled certain things differently. Maybe there are also things you said that you wish you could erase from your adult child's memories. Unfortunately, if you are reading this post, then it is likely that those regrets have shaped some of your past decisions on where and how to help your adult child. The good news is that you are open to looking at it.

So, how about stopping when you ask yourself, "What can I do to make up for the past?" Instead, start asking, "What can I do to help my adult child grow and gain more healthy independence?" The problem here is that guilt feeds on the need for immediate relief. So, the more healthy parenting you want, the more it comes from a long-term growth perspective. For example, I can think of a parent I worked with who had a nasty divorce. His way of coping was paying his adult children's bills because it temporarily assuaged his guilt. But once he looked beyond his guilt, he saw that paying for everything counted for nothing in terms of truly helping his adult children grow in both independence and emotional maturity.

article continues after advertisement

3. You're Afraid of Losing the Relationship

Yes, this one is the big one. This is exactly why I wrote my recent book, You Ruined My Life—Now You Owe Me. Many parents fear that saying no will trigger anger, rejection, or even estrangement. For example, you may resist saying no because you are afraid your adult child will go radio silent and stop communicating with you. Ironically, constant rescuing leads parents to a different problem: feeling drained and as if they can never do enough. And, worse, your adult child misses opportunities for growth and navigating life's challenges.

The Takeaway

The goal is not to love your adult child less, but rather to help them differently. Sometimes the most compassionate thing a parent can do is tolerate the discomfort of saying no. Because if you can tolerate a little more of your own uncertainty, your child may just gain a gift that never stops giving—increased independence.

item.title: Signs, Symptoms, and the Psychology of Suffering
item.description:
Imagination

Signs, Symptoms, and the Psychology of Suffering

Listening to and dialoging with the Jungian notion of the "shadow."

Posted July 23, 2026

Key points
  • In psychotherapy, symptoms are not just something to suppress as quickly as possible.
  • Working together with your therapist to discern the significance of symptoms can lead to them dissipating.
  • Even when symptoms persist, their suffering can be tolerated by better understanding them.

This is Part 5 in a series of articles describing several different methods of listening and speaking to our psychiatric symptoms in an effort to discover the crucial messages they may be trying to communicate to us.

A young C.G. Jung
Source: Wikimedia Commons

Jungian Analysis

One of the central tasks in Jungian analysis or therapy is acknowledging, confronting, and coming to terms with what Jung famously named the "shadow." According to Jung (1961), "The shadow personifies everything that the subject refuses to acknowledge about himself [sic] . . . " (p. 387), and, therefore, represses and defensively projects onto others and the world. The shadow is, by definition, unconscious, some part of ourselves of which we are unaware and do not want to know about.

From a Jungian perspective, this so-called shadow is the source of many if not most of our psychological signs, symptoms and suffering owing to its dissociation from consciousness, i.e., its unconsciousness, which makes it even more powerful and dangerous.

One of the main things that need to happen in Jungian therapy is to become more conscious or aware of our own personal shadow, the disowned or rejected part of our personality, accept responsibility for it, and integrate or incorporate it into the conscious personality as constructively as possible rather than constantly defending against it by denying or projecting these "negative" qualities, tendencies, or traits

What Is Active Imagination in Jungian Therapy?

Jung's primary method for accomplishing this daunting feat is what he called "active imagination." In active imagination, which is a phenomenon that takes place primarily in the mind's eye, the shadow can be directly confronted and deliberately spoken with. So, for example, when we experience a symptom such as inappropriate anger or rage or uncharacteristic bad behavior or dark moods in ourselves, we can be fairly sure that this is our personal shadow indirectly expressing itself and might imagine, seated or reclining with eyes closed, that we are in a room speaking with and listening to it.

We could ask: "What do you want of me?" "Why are you making my life so difficult?" Why are you causing me to behave so badly?" "Why are you continually appearing in my dreams and nightmares?" And then, again, in the mind's eye, we can give the shadow a voice with which to respond to these legitimate queries, concerns, and accusations. What will it say? And are we really ready to hear it?

article continues after advertisement

Why Is Integrating the Shadow Important?

The shadow, as an integral, vital, and essential part of ourselves, has every right to exist and express itself both in the personality and the world; when it is not allowed by us or others to do so, signs and symptoms appear seemingly compelling us to pay attention to it. The shadow becomes most dangerous and potentially evil when it remains repressed, hidden, and projected rather than accepted as part of ourselves.

For example, in the classic tale of Dr. Jekyll and Mr. Hyde, written by Robert Louis Stevenson subsequent to a dream, the evil Mr. Hyde (hide) can be seen as the good Dr. Jekyll's dissociated and denied shadow. Without his shadow Jekyll, like all of us, is only half a person. He is neither whole nor balanced. Which becomes a source of psychiatric signs and symptoms such as depression or anxiety. The goal in this phase of Jungian analysis is wholeness, to establish and cultivate a more conscious connection and relationship between the ego or persona and the shadow.

Ultimately, as with any intimate relationship, the inner relationship with the shadow must be worked out and cultivated so as to be cooperative and mutually beneficial rather than adversarial, though there are times when one must "have it out" with the shadow as regards whether and how it will be expressed. For whenever the shadow is chronically denied, the intrinsic capacity for evil is constellated and activated, as tragically evidenced in the case of Dr. Jekyll. But the shadow consists not only of negative traits and impulses but, as Jung (1961) himself puts it, "The shadow behaves compensatorily to consciousness; hence its effects can be positive as well as negative.

. . . If it has been believed hitherto that the human shadow was the source of all evil, it can now be ascertained . . . that the unconscious man [sic], that is, his shadow, does not consist only of morally reprehensible tendencies, but also displays a number of good qualities, such as normal instincts, appropriate reactions, realistic insights, creative impulses, etc." Responsibly and consciously integrating and assimilating one's personal shadow, painful though it may be to the ego and persona (the idealized way we see ourselves and wish others to see us) can be a deeply enriching, invigorating, and life-enhancing experience.

article continues after advertisement

This same active imagination method can be employed with other aspects or components of the unconscious such as the anima or animus, the inner child, and what Jung called the Self, which transcends and subsumes the ego. Active imagination can also be used when working with dreams (the shadow, said Jung, usually appears as the same gender as the dreamer) or to engage in imaginary conversation with a particular symptom in order to discern its possible meaning and message regarding wholeness and individuation (becoming one's true self).

It is commonly accompanied by the process of writing about or otherwise recording what comes up following, or sometimes during, active imagination. Indeed, writing, drawing, or painting, and creative expression in itself can be another effective technique for entering into dialogue with one's shadow and symptoms.

How Are Complexes Related to Symptoms in Jungian Psychology?

For Jung, signs or symptoms can also be expressions more specifically of personal or collective complexes, unconscious constellations of powerful feelings and memories that, when triggered by outer or inner events, cause emotional, distressing, or inappropriate reactions.

In this sense, symptoms can be utilized to discover the contents of these specific complexes (e.g., the so called inner child) and, by making the complex more conscious, mitigate the symptoms emanating from it by engaging in active imagination to dialog with the complex (see my prior post). But, in the final analysis, it is crucial to keep in mind that, as Jung noted, we all have a shadow and we all have complexes, and, as a consequence, we all suffer from some sort of symptoms from time to time and always will.

item.title: Unjournaling: Why Some People Heal Better Without Writing
item.description:
Wisdom

Unjournaling: Why Some People Heal Better Without Writing

Sometimes growth comes from participating in life rather than documenting it.

Posted July 23, 2026

Key points
  • Journaling can support wellbeing, but for some people it may reinforce rumination.
  • Constant self-documentation can keep attention focused on problems rather than experiences.
  • Unjournaling means choosing alternative ways to process emotions when writing no longer helps.
Source: Towfiqu barbhuiya / Pexels

This post began while I was packing boxes to move to a new home.

As I emptied cupboards and shelves, I came across a stack of journals I had accumulated during my years in this house. Some were filled. Others contained only a few pages. Several were completely untouched.

There were gratitude journals, travel journals, notebooks bought during optimistic New Year sales, and beautifully bound journals purchased because I was convinced that this one would finally help me become a more reflective, organized, and insightful person.

As I stacked them together, one word came to mind: Unjournaling.

Not because journaling is bad. I have journaled on and off for years. Rather, I wondered whether we have become so focused on documenting our lives that we sometimes forget to live them.

The Business of Writing Ourselves Better

Journaling has evolved from a simple reflective practice into a thriving industry.

The U.S. stationery market alone was valued at nearly $60 billion in 2025 and is projected to continue growing over the next decade, driven in part by increased interest in journaling, planners, and self-improvement products (Market Data Forecast, 2026). The broader global stationery market exceeded $165 billion in 2025 (Fortune Business Insights, 2026). At the same time, companies built around premium journals and planners have experienced remarkable growth. Papier, for example, reported annual sales exceeding £40 million by 2026 (Business Insider, 2026).

There is nothing wrong with buying a notebook. I have bought myself plenty.

Yet standing in a room surrounded by journals—many barely used—I found myself wondering how much of the self-improvement industry depends on convincing us that personal growth is only one purchase away.

The message is subtle but powerful: buy another journal, track another habit, answer another prompt, and you might finally become the person you want to be.

article continues after advertisement

When Reflection Becomes Rumination

Research suggests that expressive writing can improve well-being and help people process experiences. However, the benefits are not universal and often depend on how journaling is used (Hoult et al., 2025).

For some people, journaling creates clarity. For others, it can become a form of rumination.

I have certainly experienced both.

There have been times when writing helped me understand what I was feeling. There have also been times when I wrote the same story repeatedly, hoping that one more page would provide an answer that never came.

Many of us have experienced this. We revisit the same disappointment, relationship, mistake, or worry, believing that deeper analysis will bring relief. Instead, we remain trapped in a cycle of self-observation.

The notebook becomes less a place for discovery and more a place where distress is rehearsed.

What Is Unjournaling?

Unjournaling is not the opposite of journaling.

It is the recognition that not every experience needs to be recorded, analysed, or turned into a lesson.

Sometimes healing occurs through engagement rather than reflection.

Unjournaling might involve taking photographs instead of writing. It might mean going for a walk without mentally composing a journal entry afterwards. It could mean having a conversation, travelling somewhere new, gardening, dancing, exercising, volunteering, or simply allowing an experience to exist without trying to capture it.

article continues after advertisement

In a culture obsessed with documentation, unjournaling is the radical act of participation.

The Limits of Language

Some of the most important experiences of our lives resist words.

Illness. Recovery. Grief. Migration. Love. Identity change.

Perhaps that is why we are drawn to journals: We hope that if we can document an experience clearly enough, we might finally understand it. We write about who we were, what happened, and who we are trying to become.

But not every transformation can be captured in sentences.

Some changes reveal themselves slowly through the lives we build afterwards: the people we meet, the places we go, the risks we take, and the moments that quietly reshape us.

We do not always think our way into a new identity. Sometimes we live our way into one.

Often, meaning arrives long after the journal entry ends.

Closing the Notebook

I still own journals. I will probably buy more. But as I packed away years of notebooks, I realised something important: The moments that changed me most were rarely the ones I wrote about; they were the ones I lived.

Journaling can be a powerful tool but it is not the only growth path, nor should it become another task on an endless self-improvement checklist.

Sometimes growth happens on the page, and sometimes it happens when we close the notebook, step outside, and allow life to write the next chapter for us.

item.title: Can You Trust the Mental Health Advice You’re Reading?
item.description:
Artificial Intelligence

Can You Trust the Mental Health Advice You’re Reading?

A psychologist who specialises in mental health content shares what to check when you search.

Posted July 23, 2026

Key points
  • Credentials, citations, and originality are what Google checks for first.
  • Several easy-to-spot signals can flag unreliable content before you read it.
  • We correctly identify AI-generated text only 57% of the time.
Not everything that reads like expertise is expertise.
Source: Karl Moore / Unsplash

The Problem No One Taught Us to Solve

Mental health content is everywhere. It arrives on your feed before you've asked for it, sounds credible enough to act on, and rarely tells you how to verify it.

We were taught to be sceptical of obvious misinformation. Nobody prepared us for content that is fluent, warm, structured, and subtly wrong.

To understand what reliable mental health content actually looks like from the inside, I spoke with Emma Loker, a licensed therapist specialized in child and adolescent therapy, and CEO of PsychWrite, who works at the intersection of clinical accuracy and digital communication.

What Google Is Checking

I asked Emma what Google looks for when deciding whether a piece of mental health content is trustworthy. Her answer was more concrete than most readers would expect.

"First and foremost, Google checks whether the information is accurate and evidence-based," she told me. "Any factual errors, or a lack of research, affect trustworthiness. Google also checks that the author is a mental health expert, their expertise, experience, and qualifications. If these details aren't present, the piece loses credibility points."

It isn't only about the content itself. The website's overall reputation factors in too. And original content that adds clinical value, rather than restating what already exists, earns further trust. "Using clinical experience and judgement can help your content stand apart," Emma says. "AI can produce information that's been written hundreds of times before. That's no longer enough."

The Signals Worth Learning to Spot

When I asked Emma what a regular reader, with no SEO background, could actually look out for, her list was specific enough to be immediately useful.

Watch for: vague, flowing language that sounds meaningful but contains few concrete details. Watch for references to studies that aren't linked, don't exist, or have unusual-looking URLs. Watch for phrases like "In today's world" or "In our digital age," or a heavy reliance on words like "foster," "navigate," and "empower." Watch for information repeated across the same piece, slightly reworded, as though padding out a word count.

"The structure also gives it away," Emma adds. "Lots of bulleted lists, one after another. Metaphors stacked on metaphors. And 'It's not this, it's this' phrasing, where a complex idea is presented as a simple binary without any actual evidence."

What AI Content Looks Like

Emma gave me a direct comparison that I think is the clearest demonstration of the difference.

article continues after advertisement

An AI version of a sentence about anxiety might read: "In today's increasingly complex world, anxiety has quietly become one of the most prevalent mental health concerns affecting individuals from all walks of life." It is grammatically correct. It sounds professional. It says almost nothing.

A human, evidence-based version of the same idea would look closer to: "Anxiety disorders affect many of us. Stats show that 359 million people manage an anxiety disorder day-to-day (WHO, 2025). Fortunately, these conditions don't have to be a life sentence. Therapy, medication, and lifestyle changes can help."

The difference isn't style. It's specificity, evidence, and the presence of a real source.

Why This Is Harder Than It Sounds

Part of what makes this difficult is that most of us aren't reliable detectors. Research published in 2025 found that both human evaluators and AI detection tools correctly identified AI-generated text only slightly better than chance, with humans reaching a recognition rate of 57% (Fiedler & Döpke, 2025). The more a human has revised AI output, the harder it becomes to identify.

The problem extends to AI assistants themselves. A 2025 study in JMIR Mental Health found that nearly one in five citations generated by GPT-4o in mental health research were entirely fabricated, and 45.4% of the remaining citations contained errors (Linardon et al., 2025). And in February 2026, a Guardian investigation found that Google's AI Overviews, shown to 2 billion people monthly, had served false and dangerous mental health advice on conditions including psychosis and eating disorders. Mind, the mental health charity, described some of the AI-generated responses as "very dangerous advice that could lead people to avoid seeking help," and promptly launched a year-long global inquiry into AI and mental health as a result.

AI can sound authoritative. That isn't the same as being accurate.

This connects directly to something I wrote about recently on this page: As research on social media and mental health continues to grow (including a striking new study on how depression changes the way people respond to likes online), the quality of how that research gets communicated to the public matters more than ever.

article continues after advertisement

One Habit Worth Building

I asked Emma what single habit she would teach someone scrolling for mental health advice late at night.

"Check the credibility markers," she said. "Ensure any advice was written by someone trained to offer it: a therapist, psychologist, psychiatrist, or other mental health expert. Check for a reference section or that the page cites research. If it doesn't, and there are no sources in sight, it's likely not evidence-based."

Her second suggestion: cross-check. If multiple reputable websites make the same claims and cite relevant research, they're likely accurate. If a piece stands alone, that's worth noticing.

The content that sounds most certain is not always the content that has been most carefully checked.

item.title: Kristen Bell, Stoicism, and People-Pleasing
item.description:
Ethics and Morality

Kristen Bell, Stoicism, and People-Pleasing

What would a Stoic have to say about people-pleasing?

Posted July 23, 2026

Key points
  • Today's Stoicism is easily associated with self-help, but it is not quite the same.
  • Stoicism suggests that we should always be aiming for virtue, which means that virtue becomes our priority.
  • When we place the focus on what is genuinely good, familiar problems like people pleasing may dissipate.

At a recent leadership summit, thoughtful actor Kristen Bell was interviewed by psychologist Adam Grant. The topic was people-pleasing.

Bell describes herself as a people pleaser, hypervigilant about how other people are feeling and wanting to contribute to their feeling better.

It can feel pretty terrible to be a people pleaser. Bell offers an example by acting out a scenario where she cannot get herself to explain that she wants a second coffee but without two creams. She cannot get the words out because she feels so bad about how it will come across. Because Bell is so charming, her experience is especially revealing. A people-pleasing attitude can interfere with even the most socially skilled person's ability to voice a simple preference.

What is behind this? Grant and Bell analyze the phenomenon together.

What is people-pleasing really about?

Bell explains how much she has thought about people-pleasing. She has begun to notice the energy wasted by it and how it only leads to pointless non-interactions with others. She has been considering whether she knows what the server actually wanted, which may simply be honest feedback so that she can make the coffee the way that Bell likes. And she suggests that her fear of upsetting others might be, instead, a desire to try to control the situation, avoiding the risk that the server might become displeased or feel hassled. The idea is that people-pleasing might seem to us to be about others, but it's actually motivated by a fear of discomfort. Adam Grant even suggests that people-pleasing is selfish.

They agree on guidance for people pleasers to put into practice:

  • Lead with inquiry rather than advocacy.
  • Show care and concern. (Bell’s take on this is to “act like a team member.”)
  • Reduce the threat level.

Is there anything controversial about this advice? Likely not! At this level of generality, all sorts of approaches to life fit with this guidance.

Yet, in just a few minutes, Bell and Grant invoke many highly philosophical concepts: emotional energy, authenticity, fear, emotional boundaries, control, niceness, selfishness. And each of these, of course, has to be assigned a value and placed in the context of our overall goals in life. When it comes to the good of each of these, no matter what surveys of others tell us, we rely on deeper accounts of life’s meaning.

Stoicism

Stoicism is one such account. Stoicism, a very complex philosophical account, has very particular, and to most of us, probably odd and counterintuitive elements. It takes pains to explain morality down to the nature of belief acquisition and up to the nature of the universe. It has been gaining appeal as writers have been distilling its lessons for use today. Sometimes, necessarily, those lessons get reduced to a warning like don’t allow other people's opinions or reactions to determine your peace of mind.

article continues after advertisement

But Stoicism puts this advice in a very particular context. The context in which Stoicism places all life advice is this: Its recommendations are for a person whose goal is actually so narrow as to be to (just) become virtuous. For this goal, other goals have to go by the wayside.

This can be easy to say but difficult to envision. So the coffee example helps.

What if the coffee is not good?

Rather than focusing on why we fear other people, the Stoics offer us something else. It will sound strange: They would say that it is the preference for a type of coffee that is the problem.

Whether it contains cream is a matter of preference, what the Stoics call a preferred indifferent. The emotional difficulty surrounding the interaction therefore reveals, the Stoics would argue, an attachment to externals. This is the mistaken evaluation of what deserves concern. The preference is not wrong, but treating its fulfillment as emotionally significant is.

Epictetus

Epictetus, the ancient Stoic, worked through practical scenarios just like Bell and Grant. One is the case of a father who is too rattled to stay with his sick child. Could his absence from her bedside be justified?

Here is the method Epictetus used to reason through the question:

  • Is your love for your child an actual good?
  • Is this good what is actually involved in justifying the decision? Does love apply in what the father is considering? Are others who love the child acting the same?
  • Would you want to be loved this way?
  • Finally, check to see if your motivations differ from the way you are representing them.
article continues after advertisement

In some ways, this seems so similar to the Bell and Grant advice. But the contrast is evident when we go back and apply Stoicism to the case of too much cream in a coffee.

You would begin with: Is your preference for coffee an actual good?

The Stoic answer: No, the coffee is not an actual good.

This demonstrates the broad divergence between Stoicism and most contemporary approaches to self-help. Yes, both ask us to change if upset over a trivial social interaction. The Stoics, too, analyze interpersonal issues that do not feel good to us. But modern self-help often looks to how we can feel (and perform) better while remaining true to ourselves. Stoicism tries to help us figure out what is ethical to do in any situation.

The Stoic proposal is that proper authenticity, emotional energy, lack of fear, boundaries, helpfulness, and wanting the right amount of control result from judging correctly what is genuinely good. Once that question is answered, many familiar problems, including people pleasing (and fear, and imposter syndrome, and timidity, and selfishness) dissipate.

As strict as Stoicism (and probably most ethical theories) seems—who wants to be thinking about ethics all of the time?—it can be more permissive than self-help. Staying quiet about unwanted coffee might be the right thing to do in a situation; you would not have to feel bad about it at all. And even if thinking about ethics all the time seems onerous, we are making ethical claims all of the time—for instance, that it is actually selfish to be nice. The Stoics would say: So do that with care.

I certainly do not know if Stoic methods work to reduce anxiety and discomfort, but their idea is that having one goal rather than very many is what we should try.

Bell's line about being a team member was particularly resonant, as Marcus Aurelius recorded something similar: "We were born to work together like feet, hands, and eyes, like the two rows of teeth, upper and lower. To obstruct each other is unnatural. To feel anger at someone, to turn your back on him: these are obstructions.”

item.title: When Politics Is Personal
item.description:
Politics

When Politics Is Personal

How polarization takes a toll on young adults’ mental health.

Posted July 23, 2026

Key points
  • The mental health of young adults is negatively impacted by political polarization.
  • Creating social support is a protective factor to stress from political polarization.
  • Having someone to talk creates a sense of belonging.
  • Young adults struggling with mental health need safe spaces to talk about polarization.

We all know the three things you don’t talk about around the dinner table: money, religion, and politics. But do these once-sacred dinner-party rules still apply to Gen Z?

Religion isn’t the potentially hot-button issue it once was, with 28% of Americans identifying as religiously unaffiliated, and only 3 in 10 reporting they attend religious services regularly. Studies also show Gen Z and millennials are twice as likely as their Gen X and Baby Boomers counterparts to talk about money.

If you’re beginning to notice a trend in young people’s willingness to discuss contentious topics, it comes to a full stop when we talk—or rather don’t talk—about politics.

An online survey conducted by University of South Florida student intern Imani Hartfield at my organization, Collectively, found that the cultural heirloom of not talking politics has been passed down to yet another generation. 63% of the Gen Z respondents reported that politics had made relationships in their lives more tense. Yet, unlike in the pre-screen days, this generation feels that there is no escape from politics. With political content chasing young adults around social media, it’s no wonder their mental health has taken a hit.

Perception Versus Reality

It feels like no one can agree on anything nowadays. But is it possible that this is truly more of a feeling than an actuality? Pew Research found that 80% of adults think that Americans disagree not only on policy but also on basic facts. With the majority of Americans feeling this way it can be easy to feel as though there is no hope for reconciliation. But the reality isn’t as polarized as we think. The overwhelming majority of Americans agree that climate change is real, vaccines save lives, and that we need stricter gun control laws. Yet when we’re in our echo chambers, it can feel like everyone who voted for that other guy (or gal) lives in a warped reality.

It’s this perception of a disjointed America that leaves so many young people lonely, anxiety-ridden, and lacking a sense of belonging.

More Than a Disagreement

Sometimes, disagreeing about tax policy isn’t just about the numbers. Now, when we argue with one another, many feel as though the policy isn’t being attacked, but our identity is.

When you believe the other side doesn't just see things differently but is actively dangerous, every political conversation carries a weight it probably shouldn't. Young adults are feeling this impact as 62% of those surveyed by Collectively found that politics has negatively impacted their relationships.

Things Left Unsaid

Perhaps the best way to overcome this polarization is by having conversations. Exposing yourself to those with different points of view in a civil manner has a way of humanizing one another. Doing so allows you to understand others and empathize. Yet despite being more ostensibly connected than ever before, while many young people feel safe voicing their opinions, a majority of them choose not to, citing the desire to prevent an altercation.

article continues after advertisement

What this suggests is that avoidance has become so habitual, so automatic, that it no longer requires a specific threat to kick in. People have already internalized the calculus: is this conversation worth the risk? More often than not, the answer is NO!. And while that might preserve short-term harmony, it quietly chips away at something important, the sense that you can be honest with the people in your life without it costing you something.

The Role of Social Media

Nobody is particularly surprised to learn that doom-scrolling through political content can give you the ick. But the survey data solidifies this feeling. 65% of participants in the Collectively study reported that political posts online leave them feeling stressed or anxious.

This may not be such an issue if we used social media to supplement our social lives instead of replacing them, but with Gen Z spending about 5 hours every day on social media, more people are choosing to binge polarizing content instead of having nuanced sit-down discussions.

The Buddy System

The antidote to political venom is a friend. 85% of respondents said they have at least one person in their lives that they can discuss politics with, without fear of jeopardizing the relationship.

That's not a small thing. Social support is one of the most well-documented buffers against the psychological effects of chronic stress, and it doesn't take a village to make a difference. One person is often enough.

There's also something interesting in the data around in-group connection: for many respondents, talking with like-minded friends actually increased their sense of belonging. Polarization strains cross-group relationships, no question. But it can also pull people closer to those they already feel safe with. That's not a perfect solution, but it's a real one.

article continues after advertisement

Where to Go From Here

This research is a reminder that political polarization isn't just a problem for democracy, it's a problem for people. Individual people, with bodies that carry stress and relationships that need honesty and minds that need rest.

If you're a therapist, it's worth asking clients whether political stress is showing up in their lives in ways they haven't labeled as stress. If you're an educator or a manager or just someone who runs meetings, it's worth thinking about whether the spaces you create actually feel safe enough for honest conversation.

And if you're one of the young adults this study describes, it might be worth finding your one person. The one you can actually talk to. You may think it's a small thing, but sometimes having that one person to talk to is everything.
